INTRO_TITLE: Use Case: Publicity Stunts & Cheeky PR Campaigns
INTRO_COL1: Oddtoe is an experiential design and generative-AI animation studio based in Melbourne, creating projection, installation, and animated work for events, venues, and galleries. This is a use case: how a campaign uses Oddtoe to pull off a publicity stunt or a cheeky PR campaign, from the first idea to the photograph that gets printed. The worked example is a set of carried heads. The same steps apply to an inflatable politician, projected animation for a protest, an ironic mascot costume, or a kinetic sculpture.
INTRO_COL2: Come to Oddtoe for visual art with a point, designed by a political cartoonist — chief designer for a Washington DC paper, and an editorial cartoonist before that. That background matters here, because a photograph at a rally and a daily cartoon are the same problem. You get one picture to make the argument, and nobody sticks around for an explanation. The stunts people remember passed that test: the Trump baby blimp over Parliament Square, or the pink boat Extinction Rebellion parked in Oxford Circus.
DRAWINGS_KICKER: Let's look at three steps in the process...
DRAWINGS_INTRO: Oddtoe can handle the first three stages of a stunt — where the idea starts, how it gets designed (sketches, 3D CAD), and how people, your staff or contractors, carry and handle the protest or publicity stunt artwork.
DRAW1_BODY: I do love this stage. What could that front-page photo look like? How can your brand or movement go viral? Art and humour are Oddtoe's thing. The idea, the feeling the art stirs, and your organisation's message all get worked out here.
DRAW2_BODY: Everything starts on paper, on a grid. Proportions get argued out flat, front and side, long before anything gets cut. Here, a series of politicians' heads are sketched with the poles that the protesters will carry. Get the sketch right and the impact of the art shows for the first time.
DRAW3_BODY: Working out how anyone actually carries the art. Where they stand, how many people it takes, how the weight sits on a shoulder after an hour, whether it can turn a corner without a traffic jam forming. Oddtoe works out the carrying and the moving for you. Leave it until the morning of the march and you are solving it in a crowd.

PANEL_TITLE: What a Stunt Does to Your Numbers
PANEL_INTRO: A politician’s face at balloon scale, parked where a rally is already going on. Nobody had to stage anything. Out come the phones. So what does a stunt like this do for your numbers? Quite a lot, and all of it can be counted: coverage, shares, search traffic in the two days after, and the figures your board actually reads.
PANEL_ITEM1_TEXT: Outlets that ran the picture, and how many people they reach
PANEL_ITEM2_TEXT: You should see a spike on the day, and the photos appearing in memes and controversial posts.
PANEL_ITEM3_TEXT: Enquiries, donations or sign-ups against the same week
PANEL_OUTRO: I like the tracking in place before the day. Oddtoe shares a founder with the Datalabs Agency, a data visualisation studio, so a dashboard that shows whether the stunt worked can be part of the job.
CIRCLES_TITLE: 6 IDEAS FOR YOUR NEXT RALLY OR PUBLICITY STUNT
CIRCLES_SUB: Six ways to be the photograph the news runs. Roll over a circle and pick the one your organisation could pull off.
CIRCLES_FOOT: Want one of these for your organisation? Send the date and the message. More cheek in the gag cartoons.
CIRCLE1_TITLE: The Monument That Turns Up Uninvited
CIRCLE1_BODY: A carved head the size of a house arrives on a truck at dawn, stands in the square for one day with a banner down its side, and leaves before anyone can hold a meeting about it. The photograph is the meeting.
CIRCLE2_TITLE: The Balloon That Follows The Roadshow
CIRCLE2_BODY: They are touring their listening sessions. A balloon-scale caricature gets to every stop first and sits in the background of every photo. By the third city the balloon is the story.
CIRCLE3_BODY: The same few faces, made a hundred times over and worn by a hundred volunteers queuing outside the housing office. From across the street it reads as everyone, and from a drone it reads as a wall.
CIRCLE4_TITLE: The Big Thing In A Marginal Seat
CIRCLE4_BODY: Australia loves a Big Thing, so build one. A three-storey inflatable of whatever the policy hurts, parked in a Bunnings car park in the seat that decides the election, with a plaque and a picnic table.
CIRCLE5_BODY: Giant eyeballs in a clear bubble on the lawn outside the department for the week of the decision. Nobody needs the sign. Everyone photographs it with the building behind.
CIRCLE6_TITLE: Gag Cartoons That Start An Argument
CIRCLE6_BODY: One panel a day for the length of the campaign, drawn by a former political cartoonist and animated for social. The kind of joke that gets a minister’s office to ring the paper. That phone call is your coverage.
WHO_KICKER: Campaigns, PR agencies, unions, and NGOs
WHO_COL1: Non-profits and NGOs, grassroots campaigns, unions, advocacy organisations, political campaigns, and PR agencies with a brand that wants a publicity stunt. What they all have is a date in the diary and something they need people to see. Campaigns with a fixed date — a launch, a vote, a summit — need one day to produce a month of coverage. Unions want objects that come out again and again, because the same members turn up several times a year.
WHO_COL2: NGOs and advocacy organisations need artwork that still works when volunteers in three cities are running it and there is no designer in the room. That means artwork files anyone can pick up. Political campaigns buy artwork and objects the way they buy everything else. Oddtoe has done fundraiser illustration for a US House candidate. Agencies working for any of the above are welcome too: see experiential marketing.
TIMELINE_TITLE: A STUNT, FROM BRIEF TO FRONT PAGE
STEP1_TITLE: Every rally looks like every rally
STEP1_BODY: Placards, a banner, a megaphone, and a photographer who has shot it four hundred times. A news editor scrolls straight past. Led By Donkeys got famous by putting politicians’ own words on billboards, and it worked because the joke took one second to get. So before anything gets drawn we settle one question: what does this photograph have to say?
STEP1_CRAFT: Editorial judgement, from years of drawing to a deadline
STEP1_CAPTION: The idea, before anyone has measured a thing
STEP2_BODY: Cartoons first, because that is where the joke lives. In this example it is four oversized heads of the people the campaign is up against. Whatever the object is, it has to read from thirty metres away, over a crowd, and still work cropped square on a phone. You approve it on paper before anything gets built.
STEP2_CAPTION: The heads drawn flat, with figures for scale
STEP3_TITLE: Designed in Melbourne, built wherever it needs to be
STEP3_BODY: Design happens in Melbourne. The build happens wherever makes sense for the job: my own workshop for a carried piece, a specialist maker for an inflatable or a costume, or a fabricator near you working from the drawings. Whatever it is, it is built light enough to carry, finished so it photographs without glare, and crated so it can be shipped.
STEP4_BODY: Out of the crate, onto shoulders, into the photograph. No rigging, no power, no technician on a headset. A few volunteers and a march route are the whole production.
STEP4_CRAFT: Built to be carried, not installed
STEP4_CAPTION: Out of the crate and into the street
STEP5_BODY: A news editor runs the photograph that does not look like the other twelve. That is what the object is for — being the reason an editor picks your rally over someone else’s. And the campaign gets its own photos and video, instead of relying on whoever happened to turn up.
STEP5_CRAFT: Photos and video the campaign owns
STEP6_BODY: A stage costs money once and is gone by Monday. A built object goes back in the crate and comes out again at the next action, the one after that, and the AGM. That is a much easier thing for a board to sign off than a single day’s spend.
STEP6_CAPTION: Made once. Still there years later
WHY_KICKER: The bit that is not a service
WHY_COL1: Street art is punk rock for visual artists. You do not need a gallery or a commission or anyone’s permission, and it gets seen by people who never decided to look at art that day. That is most of why this subject grabs me. A head carried down a street is doing the same job as a paste-up on a wall at four in the morning — putting the argument where people actually are.
WHY_COL2: I make my own work as well as client work, and sculpture street art is where I want to take that next. So when a publicity stunt brief comes in, it is about the closest thing to what I would be making anyway. The practical upside for a campaign is that the person designing the object has a stake in whether it works. I want the photograph to be good for the same reason you do.

WYG_KICKER: Objects, artwork, and the footage afterwards
WYG_TITLE: What Does a Campaign Actually Get?
WYG_COL1: The object, the artwork it came from, and the photos and video from the day. All of it is yours to keep, crate included, and it goes out again at the next action. • The object — in this example four oversized heads, built light enough to carry • The character artwork — the same designs flat, for placards, posters and social • A crate it packs into and travels in • Photos and video from the day, ready for news editors and for phones
WYG_COL2: People tend to forget about the artwork. Because the object is built from finished character designs, the campaign also owns drawings that work on a poster, a placard, a t-shirt and a phone screen without redrawing anything. It can be whatever the idea needs: carried heads, a giant inflatable, a mascot costume, a kinetic sculpture, or a projection on a building after dark, with the same characters animated. They are designed together, so what goes up on the wall is the same character as the one in the street.
PKG1_BODY: We work out what the action needs to look like before we work out what to build. Bring a date, a message and whatever you already have.
PKG2_KICKER: Drawn until you can see it
PKG2_BODY: Character art, scale drawings, and the object shown where it will stand. You sign off on a picture of the thing, at the size it will be.
PKG3_BODY: Construction and weight. How volunteers move it. Customs, quarantine and freight, if it travels. And the date, which nobody can move.
PKG4_BODY: Designed in Melbourne, built by the right maker for the piece, here or near you. Finished so it photographs without glare, and made to come apart into a crate and go back together without a technician.
PKG5_BODY: I run the job myself: visual progress reports, an action plan against your date, and a press plan for the day, worked out with whoever handles your press.
CRED_COL1: A political cartoon and a publicity stunt photograph do the same job. You get about a second of someone’s attention, and if the picture needs explaining you have already lost them. Oddtoe drew editorial cartoons at college in Delaware, then worked as political cartoonist and chief designer for a Washington DC paper. Years of picking which single image a political story runs with, and watching an editor bin the ones that missed, usually for being too clever.
CRED_COL2: More recently, an illustration and cover design for a US House candidate’s fundraiser — a donkey bullying an elephant. Blunt, and it still reads printed small. The same instinct decides what a stunt object should be. Out of twelve photographs from twelve actions, a news editor runs one. The job is to be that one. It also decides what to leave out. A head that needs a caption has failed, and so does one that turns into a blob from across a square.

FAQ.q: What does this publicity stunt use case cover?
FAQ.a: A worked example of a publicity stunt. It follows one brief - a campaign with a press day and no picture - from the first question through design, fabrication, the day itself, and what the campaign still owns afterwards. It uses carried heads as the example, and an inflatable, a projection, a mascot costume or a kinetic sculpture would follow the same shape.

FAQ.q: How long does a publicity stunt take?
FAQ.a: Six to eight weeks from brief to press day for a carried piece. Design and approval take the first fortnight, fabrication the next three weeks, and the rest is packing and freight. An inflatable or a mascot costume takes longer, because a specialist maker builds it from the drawings. A rush is possible but it comes out of the design stage, which is the part worth protecting.

FAQ.q: Can it be shipped outside Australia?
FAQ.a: Usually, yes. Pieces are designed to crate, and freight and customs get worked through with a freight agent as part of the job, including any treatment or certification the materials need. Often the simpler answer is to build near you, working from the drawings.

FAQ.q: What does a publicity stunt cost?
FAQ.a: Oddtoe does not publish prices. Cost is driven by what the object is, how many, how large, how much structure each one needs, and where it has to travel. It is costed the same way as any other prop fabrication job. Send the brief and the date and you get a quote.

Maybe. It depends on the city, the site, the size of the object and what else is happening that day, and I am not the person to rule on it from here. What I can do is work through it with your team early, and with the council or the venue if it comes to that, so it is settled long before the week of the stunt.

FAQ.q: Can we use it more than once?
FAQ.a: That is the point. It goes back in the crate and comes out at the next action. Used a few times, one build can cost less than hiring something new for each one.

FAQ.q: Can you do the animation and projection as well?
FAQ.a: Yes, and they are designed together when the brief calls for it - the same characters animated and projected after dark. See projection art and generative AI animation.
